source.title: Not All Features Are Created Equal: A Mechanistic Study of Vision-Language-Action Models
source.authors: Bryce Grant; Xijia Zhao; Peng Wang

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses SAEs to analyze VLA representations, motivating them with the general idea that dense activations can be polysemantic, but it does not test whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: Appendix F.2 reports FFN-neuron associations with token categories based on weight projections, including counts by layer. It does not measure whether a neuron responds strongly to several unrelated inputs or test whether those responses share a feature the model uses. SAE pooling and ablation results concern SAE reconstructions or features, not neuron polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The paper cites the idea that dense activations are polysemantic only to motivate SAEs, then reports VLA intervention and SAE results. Its only neuron-level analysis (App. F.2) counts FFN neurons by weight projection onto token categories. It never measures whether single neurons respond to unrelated inputs, reports no polysemantic share, and tests no cause, architecture effect or measurement dependence.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that fine-tuned VLAs encode coordinate-bound motor programs, selected from the scene and executed by the expert pathway where one exists. They find language is used mainly when vision is ambiguous, and that the goal sits in the VLM pathway. They also conclude that SAE pooling should be chosen per architecture and signal, and that temporal-contrastive SAEs hurt every architecture tested.
record.recipe_differences: No comparable method for testing neuron polysemanticity is used; the paper applies activation interventions, SAEs, and token-vocabulary projections to study VLA behavior and representations.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE reconstruction outcomes vary with pooling method and architecture, but the paper does not test sensitivity of neuron-polysemanticity measurement to these choices.

fits_no_version.finding: FFN neurons in π0.5's PaliGemma and OFT's Llama-2 are mapped by weight projection to motion, object, gripper, direction and spatial token categories. Category shares shift across layers. OFT concept counts imply neurons carry multiple concept labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In fine-tuned VLA backbones, weight-projection token-category associations of FFN neurons shift with depth, from object/spatial toward motion/gripper in π0.5. In OFT, neurons appear to associate with several related concepts.

record.problems: The neuron-category results use FFN weight projections onto a token-association vocabulary rather than functional response tests; the paper does not report category overlap or a polysemantic-neuron rate.

untested.parts: No share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts. The F.2 counts are category associations from weight projection in VLA backbones.
No test of superposition as the cause.
No test of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
Architecture comparisons concern SAE pooling and injection override, not polysemantic-neuron share.
No test of whether mixed neuron responses reflect one shared feature.
No test of how activation range or explanation scoring changes polysemantic counts.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its single-feature ablation results (28–92% zero effect, read as redundantly distributed concepts) concern SAE features, not neurons, so they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No image-classifier neuron response test or analysis of the cited InceptionV1 neuron.
The paper does not measure the share of transformer-language-model MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
No test of superposition or feature-to-neuron capacity pressure as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
The paper compares VLA architectures and SAE pooling choices, but does not measure how architecture, activation function, or regularization changes the share of polysemantic neurons.
No test of whether apparently mixed neuron responses share a coherent feature or job.
The paper compares SAE pooling and reconstruction outcomes, not how neuron polysemanticity counts vary with activation-range selection or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: π0.5 (PaliGemma FFN)
rows.operation_detail: Projected FFN weight vectors onto a token-association vocabulary and counted neuron associations by category.
rows.measure: Number and share of neurons associated with each listed token category
rows.value: Motion verbs: 4,231 (25.8%); gripper state: 998 (6.1%); objects: 3,660 (22.3%); spatial relations: 1,655 (10.1%).
rows.locator: Appendix F.2, FFN Motor Primitive Neurons
rows.note: These are vocabulary-projection associations, not measured activation responses to unrelated inputs; the paper does not state whether category assignments overlap.
rows.check: The listed category shares sum to about 64%, so whether categories overlap or cover all neurons is unreadable. These are vocabulary-projection associations, not activation responses. Linking the row to no version is correct.

rows.subject: π0.5 (PaliGemma FFN)
rows.operation_detail: Projected FFN weight vectors onto a token-association vocabulary and counted neuron associations by category.
rows.measure: Number and share of neurons associated with each listed token category
rows.value: Motion verbs: 6,606 (40.3%); objects: 2,907 (17.7%); gripper state: 2,989 (18.2%); direction: 2,223 (13.6%); spatial relations: 1,151 (7.0%).
rows.locator: Appendix F.2, FFN Motor Primitive Neurons
rows.note: The paper reports that the motion-verb count rises from 4,231 (25.8%) at layer 0 and the gripper-state count from 998 (6.1%); object and spatial-relation counts fall from 3,660 (22.3%) and 1,655 (10.1%), respectively. This does not establish functional polysemanticity.
rows.check: The shares sum to about 97%, and the paper does not say whether neurons belong to more than one category. These are weight-projection associations in a VLA's PaliGemma FFN, not a polysemanticity rate. Linking the row to no version is correct.

rows.subject: OpenVLA-OFT (Llama-2)
rows.operation_detail: Mapped neurons to token concepts at each layer.
rows.measure: Neuron counts associated with selected spatial and object token concepts across layers
rows.value: Spatial_in neurons: 5,483 → 7,245; spatial_on neurons: 4,724 → 6,727; obj_can neurons: 814 → 1,175, from layer 0 to layer 31.
rows.locator: Appendix F.2, FFN Motor Primitive Neurons
rows.note: The paper says the spatial counts grow monotonically and object neurons remain sparse. These are concept-mapping counts, not tests of responses to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: Layer-31 counts for spatial_in (7,245) and spatial_on (6,727) together exceed the 11,008 neurons per layer, so neurons must carry several concept labels. Those labels come from weight-projection association, and in/on are related spatial concepts, so this does not show a response to unrelated inputs. Linking the row to no version is correct.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
